name: GYS1 (PSSM1)
summary: GYS1, glycogen synthase 1, on chromosome 10: the muscle enzyme that builds glycogen. One missense change, c.925G>A (p.Arg309His, also written R309H), leaves the enzyme permanently overactive and causes type 1 polysaccharide storage myopathy (PSSM1): muscle stores too much glycogen and an abnormal polysaccharide. It is dominant, so one copy is enough and there is no silent carrier state in the genetic sense, but penetrance is incomplete: a horse with the variant may show no signs, mild tying-up or serious exercise intolerance, depending on management, fitness, diet, sex, age and other genes. Two copies may be worse. Found in at least 30 breeds, most often in draft breeds and in Quarter Horses and related breeds, less often in Warmbloods, and reported absent from Thoroughbreds, Arabians and Standardbreds. "PSSM2" is a name for similar muscle disease in horses that test clear here; it is not an allele of GYS1. Any effect on performance comes from the disease, not from a separate effect on speed or build.

phenotypes.name: Wild type
phenotypes.description: Two working copies. Nothing is wrong and nothing is passed on.

phenotypes.name: PSSM1 (tying-up)
phenotypes.description: One copy of the PSSM1 variant. Muscle builds up too much glycogen and an abnormal polysaccharide. The horse may show nothing at all, or stiffness, cramping and tying-up after exercise, reluctance to move forward and firm, painful muscles, up to severe episodes of muscle breakdown with sweating, a fast heart rate and dark urine. How badly a horse is affected varies with management, fitness, diet, sex, age and other genes.

phenotypes.name: PSSM1 (two copies)
phenotypes.description: Two copies of the PSSM1 variant. The same disorder, and such horses may be more severely affected than those with one copy. Every foal inherits the variant.
